blocks.html: In Hypothetical Propositions you met statements built from other statements: "If it rains, then the game is canceled" contains two smaller claims. Symbolic logic starts by taking that idea seriously. Before we can write any symbols, we have to know which pieces of a sentence are the building blocks.

A simple statement makes one claim and has no other statement inside it: "Maya is at the park." A compound statement is built from one or more simpler statements with a word like not, and, or, if … then or if and only if: "Maya is at the park and Leo is at home."

A statement is compound when it has another statement as a part, joined or changed by a connective word. Otherwise it is simple. A negation such as "Maya is not at the park" counts as compound: it is built from "Maya is at the park".

Logic cares about which claims depend on which. If a statement is compound, its truth depends on the truth of its parts; "Maya is at the park and Leo is at home" is true only when both parts are. A simple statement has no parts to depend on, so in symbolic logic it gets a single letter, like $p$. Splitting sentences correctly is what makes the later rules work.

blocks.title: Find the simple parts
blocks.q: "Either the library is open or the bookstore is open." Simple or compound? If compound, what are its parts?
steps: Look for a connective word: "either … or".
It joins two claims: "the library is open" and "the bookstore is open".
Each of those has no smaller statement inside it, so each is simple.

blocks.title: One relation, not two claims
blocks.q: "Ava and Ben are cousins." Simple or compound?
steps: The word "and" appears, so check what it joins.
Try splitting: "Ava is a cousin and Ben is a cousin." That is not what the sentence says; "cousin" needs someone to be a cousin of.
The sentence states one relation between two people. "And" joins two names, not two statements.

blocks.title: A hidden "not"
blocks.q: "Ava is unhappy about the rain." Simple or compound?
steps: "Un-" is part of the word "unhappy", not the connective "not".
There is no smaller statement inside it.

blocks.html: Calling "Ava and Ben are cousins" compound because of the word "and". Test it: can you rewrite the sentence as two complete claims joined by "and", each true or false on its own, without changing the meaning? "Ava and Ben finished the puzzle" passes the test (Ava finished, Ben finished). "Ava and Ben are cousins", "met at the library" or "shook hands" do not. They are simple.

blocks.html: A compound formula is built from statement letters with ¬, ∧, ∨, → and ↔. In $p \to q$, $p$ is the antecedent and $q$ the consequent; in $p \land q$ the parts are conjuncts; in $p \lor q$ they are disjuncts.

Ordinary words like "and" and "or" carry extra hints of time, contrast or emotion. "She stood up and left" suggests an order; "but" suggests a contrast. Logic keeps only what matters for truth: whether each part is true or false. That is why one symbol, $\land$, can stand for "and", "but", "although" and "yet". Each symbol has one exact meaning, set by when the compound is true.

Every formula is either a single statement letter or is built from smaller formulas by one connective. So $p$, $\neg p$, $p \land q$ and $\neg (p \land q) \to r$ are all formulas, and each of the last three was made by one final step. That recipe is what lets a computer, or you, check any formula piece by piece.

The meanings are fixed by truth tables, which you will use throughout Truth Values of the Connectives. Here is the one surprise to remember now: logical "or" is inclusive. $p \lor q$ is true when $p$ is true, when $q$ is true, and also when both are true.

blocks.title: Symbolize one connective
blocks.q: Let $p$: the library is open; $q$: the museum is open. Write "Either the library is open or the museum is open."
steps: "Either … or" is disjunction, $\lor$.
The first disjunct is $p$, the second $q$.

blocks.title: Two words, one symbol
blocks.q: With the same letters, write "The library is open, but the museum is not open."
steps: "But" claims both parts, so it is $\land$.
The second part denies $q$: $\neg q$.
Join them.

blocks.title: Name the parts
blocks.q: In $(p \land q) \to r$, what are the antecedent and the consequent?
steps: The main connective is $\to$.
Everything before it, $p \land q$, is the antecedent.
Everything after it, $r$, is the consequent.

blocks.html: Reading $\lor$ as "one or the other but not both". In logic, $p \lor q$ is true when both parts are true. If you mean "exactly one", you must say so: $(p \lor q) \land \neg (p \land q)$. A quick check: "You may have cake or ice cream" is false only if you get neither.
You may type the connectives on a keyboard as ~ (not), & (and), v or | (or), -> (if … then) and <-> (if and only if). The answer box turns them into symbols.

blocks.html: Once formulas have more than one connective, we need to know how they group. In ordinary arithmetic, $2 + 3 \times 4$ means $2 + (3 \times 4)$; in logic we avoid surprises by always writing parentheses around every binary part of a larger formula. This lesson builds on The Five Connectives.

The main connective is the one with the widest scope: the one outside all parentheses, applied last. It decides what kind of statement the whole formula is. A $\neg$ covers only what comes right after it: one letter, or one whole pair of parentheses.

A formula is built in stages, like a sentence diagram. $
eg (p \land q)$ is built by first making $p \land q$, then denying it. $
eg p \land q$ is built by first making $
eg p$, then joining it to $q$. The last step decides the kind of statement: the first is a negation, the second a conjunction. They mean different things, and a truth table will show a row where they differ.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Same letters, different scope: the columns differ in the first and last rows.

blocks.title: Find the main connective
blocks.q: What is the main connective of $(p \lor q) \to \neg r$?
steps: Cover what is inside parentheses: $p \lor q$ is one block.
What is left is block $\to$ $\neg r$.
The $\neg$ covers only $r$.
blocks.a: The conditional $\to$: the formula is a conditional.

blocks.title: A negation of a whole formula
blocks.q: What is the main connective of $\neg ((p \to q) \land r)$?
steps: The $\neg$ stands in front of a pair of parentheses that holds everything else.
So it is applied last, to the whole conjunction.
blocks.a: Negation: the formula is a negation.

blocks.title: Write the negation
blocks.q: Deny the whole formula $p \lor q$.
steps: Put $\neg$ in front.
Keep parentheses so the $\neg$ covers both disjuncts.

blocks.title: A longer formula
blocks.q: What is the main connective of $p \to (q \leftrightarrow \neg r)$? What are its two parts?
steps: The parentheses hold $q \leftrightarrow \neg r$ together as one block.
Outside them is only $p$ $\to$ block.
So the antecedent is $p$ and the consequent is $q \leftrightarrow \neg r$.

blocks.html: Why insist on parentheses around every binary part? Without them, $(p \land q) \lor r$ could mean $(p \land q) \lor r$ or $p \land (q \lor r)$, and those two disagree when $p$ is false and $r$ is true. Writing the parentheses every time removes the doubt, so two readers always see the same formula.

Dropping parentheses changes the meaning. $\neg (p \land q)$ says "not both"; $\neg p \land q$ says "not $p$, and $q$". They differ, for example, when $p$ and $q$ are both false: the first is true, the second false. When you deny a compound, always keep its parentheses.

items: Count the parentheses from the outside in.
The connective outside every pair is the main one.
If a $\neg$ stands in front of everything (with parentheses), the formula is a negation.

blocks.html: Knowing the main connective is the first step of almost every later skill: computing truth values in Computing a Truth Value, reading formulas aloud, and choosing which proof rule applies.

blocks.html: With the connectives from The Main Connective and Scope you can now translate real sentences. This lesson handles the three easiest connectives, not, and and or, and the English phrases that hide them.

head: English
Symbols

not $p$; it is not the case that $p$

blocks.html:
"But", "although" and "yet" are all $\land$. "Neither $p$ nor $q$" denies each part: $
eg p \land 
eg q$. "Not both" denies the conjunction: $
eg (p \land q)$.

Ask when the English sentence would be true. "Neither Maya nor Leo plays chess" is true only when Maya does not play and Leo does not play, which is exactly when $
eg p \land 
eg q$ is true. "Maya and Leo do not both play chess" allows one of them to play; it rules out only the case where both do. That is $
eg (p \land q)$. Translation is matching truth conditions, not matching words.

blocks.title: Neither … nor
blocks.q: Let $p$: Maya plays chess; $q$: Leo plays chess. Translate "Neither Maya nor Leo plays chess."
steps: "Neither … nor" denies both parts.
Not $p$, and not $q$.

blocks.title: Not both
blocks.q: Translate "It is not the case that both Maya and Leo play chess."
steps: The denial covers the conjunction "both $p$ and $q$".
Write the conjunction in parentheses and deny it.

blocks.title: Three parts
blocks.q: Let $r$: Ava plays chess. Translate "Maya plays chess, but neither Leo nor Ava does."
steps: The comma before "but" marks the main connective, $\land$.
The first part is $p$.
The second part is "neither $q$ nor $r$": $\neg q \land \neg r$.

blocks.title: Both denied, joined by or
blocks.q: Translate "Either Maya does not play chess or Leo does not play chess."
steps: Each part is a negation: $\neg p$ and $\neg q$.
"Either … or" joins them.
blocks.a: $\neg p \lor \neg q$, which says the same thing as "not both".

blocks.html: Notice what translation leaves out. "Maya plays chess, but Leo does not" suggests a contrast, as if we expected Leo to play. Logic keeps only the claim that both parts are true. The hint of surprise is real in conversation, but it does not change when the sentence is true, so $\land$ is the right symbol.

Writing "neither $p$ nor $q$" as $
eg p \lor 
eg q$. That formula means "not both", which is true when only one of them plays. Check with the case where Maya plays and Leo does not: "neither plays" is false, but $
eg p \lor 
eg q$ is true. The two do not match, so the translation is wrong.

blocks.html: Conditionals are the trickiest part of translation, because English has many ways to say "if … then" and some of them put the parts in reverse order. You met the basic idea in Hypothetical Propositions; here we make it exact. Throughout, $p$ stands for one simple statement and $q$ for another.

head: English
Symbols
rows: if $p$, then $q$; $q$ if $p$; $q$ provided that $p$; whenever $p$, $q$
$\neg q \to p$, which is equivalent to $p \lor q$
blocks.cap: All of these have $p$ as the antecedent.

blocks.html: "If" introduces the antecedent; "only if" introduces the consequent. A sufficient condition is the antecedent; a necessary condition is the consequent. "$p$ unless $q$" means "if not $q$, then $p$".

Think about what each sentence rules out. "You may vote only if you are registered" rules out one situation: voting while not registered. $p \to q$, with $p$: you vote and $q$: you are registered, is false in exactly that situation, $p$ true and $q$ false. The sentence does not promise that registering lets you vote, so it is not $q \to p$. The same test explains "necessary": being registered is necessary for voting because every voter is registered.

cards.text: Studying is sufficient for passing.

blocks.title: Only if
blocks.q: Let $p$: you get into the show; $q$: you have a ticket. Translate "You get into the show only if you have a ticket."
steps: "Only if" introduces the consequent: having a ticket.
So the antecedent is getting in.

blocks.title: Necessary
blocks.q: Translate "Having a ticket is necessary for getting into the show."
steps: A necessary condition is the consequent.
Getting in needs a ticket: if you get in, you have one.
blocks.a: $p \to q$ (the same claim as the last example)

blocks.title: Unless
blocks.q: Let $r$: the game goes ahead; $s$: it rains. Translate "The game goes ahead unless it rains."
steps: "$X$ unless $Y$" means "if not $Y$, then $X$".
If it does not rain, the game goes ahead.

blocks.html: Why does "unless" act like "or"? "The game goes ahead unless it rains" is broken only when it does not rain and the game still does not go ahead. $r \lor s$ is false in exactly that case too. So you may translate "unless" as $\lor$; both forms are correct.

Reversing "only if". "You pass only if you study" is pass → study, not study → pass. Reversing it is the same slip as affirming the consequent. A check: does the sentence promise that studying is enough? No, so study → pass is not what it says.

blocks.html: A biconditional joins two conditionals: $p \leftrightarrow q$ says $p \to q$ and $q \to p$ together. With it you have all five connectives, so you can now translate long sentences. The method builds on Translating Conditionals.

"$p$ if and only if $q$" and "$p$ just in case $q$" are $p \leftrightarrow q$. For a long sentence, find the main connective of the English first, then translate each part the same way, from the outside in.

"You may enter if you have a ticket" gives $t \to e$; "you may enter only if you have a ticket" gives $e \to t$. Saying both at once, "you may enter if and only if you have a ticket", claims both conditionals, which is $e \leftrightarrow t$. Long sentences work like long formulas: the commas, "either" and "both" show which pieces belong together, just as parentheses do.

items: Mark the simple statements and give each a letter.
Find the connective that joins the two biggest pieces; commas and words like "either", "both" and "then" show the grouping.
Write that main connective with parentheses around each side.
Translate each side the same way.

blocks.title: If and only if
blocks.q: Let $p$: the store is open; $q$: the light is on. Translate "The light is on if and only if the store is open."
steps: "If and only if" is $\leftrightarrow$.
Left side: the light is on, $q$. Right side: $p$.

blocks.title: Three parts
blocks.q: Let $p$: it rains; $q$: the game is canceled; $r$: we visit the museum. Translate "If it rains and the game is canceled, then we visit the museum."
steps: The main connective is "if … then".
The antecedent is "it rains and the game is canceled": $p \land q$.
The consequent is $r$.

blocks.title: Grouping by "either"
blocks.q: Translate "Either it rains or the game is canceled, and we do not visit the museum."
steps: The comma before "and" makes $\land$ the main connective.
"Either … or" groups the first part: $p \lor q$.
The second part is $\neg r$.

blocks.title: Only if, with a compound
blocks.q: Translate "We visit the museum only if it rains and the game is canceled."
steps: "Only if" introduces the consequent.
The consequent is the conjunction $p \land q$; the antecedent is $r$.

blocks.html: Translating word by word from left to right. "If it rains, then either the game is canceled or we visit the museum" is $p \to (q \lor r)$, but reading left to right you might write $(p \to q) \lor r$, which is a different claim (it is true whenever $r$ is true, even if it rains and the game is not canceled). Find the main connective of the English first.

blocks.html: Translation runs both ways. After Biconditionals and Longer Sentences, you should be able to read a formula aloud in English that keeps its exact meaning. This is how you check your own translations, and how you explain a proof to someone who does not read symbols.

Read a formula from its main connective inward. Use "either … or" for $\lor$, "both … and" for $\land$ inside a larger formula, "if … then" for $\to$, and "it is not the case that" (or "not both") for a $\neg$ in front of parentheses.

English has no parentheses, so grouping words do their job. "Either $p$ or $q$, and $r$" groups the disjunction, while "$p$, or both $q$ and $r$" groups the conjunction. The phrases "either", "both" and "it is not the case that" open a group just as "(" does; the comma or "then" closes it. Without them, the English is ambiguous, and an ambiguous sentence cannot be checked.

head: Formula
A faithful reading
rows: It is not the case that both $p$ and $q$ (not both $p$ and $q$).
blocks.cap: Grouping words take the place of parentheses.

blocks.title: Not both
blocks.q: Let $p$: the oven is hot; $q$: the dough has risen. Read $\neg (p \land q)$ in English.
steps: The main connective is the $\neg$ in front of the parentheses.
It denies the conjunction as a whole.
blocks.a: It is not the case that both the oven is hot and the dough has risen.

blocks.title: A conditional with a compound antecedent
blocks.q: With $r$: the bread bakes, read $(p \land q) \to r$.
steps: Main connective: $\to$.
Antecedent: both $p$ and $q$.
blocks.a: If both the oven is hot and the dough has risen, then the bread bakes.

blocks.title: Check a reading
blocks.q: Someone reads $p \lor (q \land r)$ as "Either the oven is hot or the dough has risen, and the bread bakes." Is that right?
steps: That English groups "either … or" first, so it says $(p \lor q) \land r$.
The formula groups $q \land r$ instead.
blocks.a: No. A faithful reading is "Either the oven is hot, or both the dough has risen and the bread bakes."

blocks.html: A good habit: after you translate a sentence into symbols, read your formula back into English with these phrases and compare it with the original. If the two sentences would be true in different situations, one of the translations has a mistake, and the reading usually shows where the grouping went wrong.

Reading $
eg (p \land q)$ as "not $p$ and not $q$". That reading says $
eg p \land 
eg q$, which is stronger. "Not both" leaves open that one of them is true. Use "it is not the case that both" or "not both" to keep the negation over the whole conjunction.

blocks.html: In The Five Connectives you learned five symbols. Now we pin down exactly what each one means. The meaning of a connective is a rule: given the truth values of the parts, it tells you the truth value of the whole. Logicians call such a rule a truth function.

Each connective is a truth function. $\neg p$ flips the value of $p$. $p \land q$ is true only when both are true. $p \lor q$ is false only when both are false. $p \to q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. $p \leftrightarrow q$ is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same value.

head: $p$
$q$
$p \land q$
$p \lor q$
$p \to q$
$p \leftrightarrow q$
blocks.cap: The four binary connectives, row by row. $\neg p$ is F when $p$ is T, and T when $p$ is F.

blocks.html: Why is a conditional true when its antecedent is false? Think of $p \to q$ as a promise: "If you finish your chores, you can go to the movies." The promise is broken in one situation only: you finish your chores and are not allowed to go. If you did not finish them, nothing was promised, so the promise was not broken. Logic counts a claim that was not broken as true. This reading is called the material conditional, and it is the one every later rule assumes.

blocks.cap: The conditional: one F, in the row where the antecedent is true and the consequent false.

blocks.title: A false antecedent
blocks.q: Let $p$ be F and $q$ be T. What is the value of $p \to q$?
steps: The only row that makes a conditional F has $p$ T and $q$ F.
Here $p$ is F, so the conditional is not broken.

blocks.title: Inclusive or
blocks.q: Let $p$ and $q$ both be T. What is $p \lor q$?
steps: A disjunction is F only when both disjuncts are F.
Here both are T.

blocks.title: The biconditional
blocks.q: Let $p$ be F and $q$ be F. What is $p \leftrightarrow q$?
steps: A biconditional is T when both sides match.
Both are F, so they match.

blocks.html: Calling $p \to q$ false, or "not applicable", when $p$ is false. In logic every formula is true or false in every row, and a conditional with a false antecedent is true. A check: the only F in the conditional column is the row T, F.

items: Negation: flip.
Conjunction: one F makes it F.
Disjunction: one T makes it T.
Conditional: F only for T → F.
Biconditional: T when the values match.

blocks.html: Because each connective is a truth function, the value of any formula, however long, is settled by the values of its letters. That is the fact behind every truth table in this unit, starting with Computing a Truth Value.

blocks.html: Every connective is a truth function (Truth Values of the Connectives), and every formula is built step by step (The Main Connective and Scope). Put those two facts together and you can find the value of any formula once you know the values of its letters.

Work from the inside out. Write the value of each letter, then the value of each smallest compound part, and keep going until you reach the main connective. Its value is the value of the whole formula.

A formula is a tree: the letters are the leaves and the main connective is the root. Each connective needs the values of its own parts before it can give a value, so the innermost parts must be done first. Working left to right ignores the tree and can apply a connective to the wrong pieces.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: One row: the part columns show the inside-out order.

blocks.title: Two letters
blocks.q: Let $p$ be T and $q$ be F. Find the value of $\neg (p \land q) \lor q$.
steps: Innermost: $p \land q$ is F (one part is F).
$\neg (p \land q)$ is T.
The main connective $\lor$ joins T and $q$ = F, giving T.

blocks.title: Three letters
blocks.q: Let $p$ be T, $q$ be F and $r$ be T. Find $(p \lor q) \to \neg r$.
steps: $p \lor q$ is T.
$\neg r$ is F.
The conditional has a T antecedent and an F consequent, so it is F.

blocks.title: A negation in front
blocks.q: With the same values, find $\neg ((p \to q) \leftrightarrow r)$.
steps: $p \to q$ is F (T → F).
$(p \to q) \leftrightarrow r$ compares F with T: different, so F.
The outer $\neg$ makes it T.

blocks.html:
Working left to right, or applying a negation to the wrong part. In $
eg p \land q$ the $
eg$ belongs to $p$ alone, but in $
eg (p \land q)$ it belongs to the whole conjunction. Before you compute, find the main connective and the scope of each $
eg$; then write the value of every part under its connective, as the table above does.

Writing each part's value under its connective is not busywork. It lets you, or anyone checking your work, find a slip in a single step instead of redoing the whole formula. Longer formulas need nothing new, only more parts. A formula with ten connectives takes ten small steps, each one a look-up in the table of the connective.

A good check at the end: look at the main connective and ask whether the value you got makes sense for it. A conjunction you marked T must have both parts T; a conditional you marked F must have a true antecedent and a false consequent. If not, one of the inside steps went wrong.
The same method answers questions about parts: the value of $p \to r$ inside $(p \to r) \land q$ is just the value you wrote under that arrow on the way up.

blocks.html: In Computing a Truth Value you found a formula's value in one row. A truth table does that for every possible row at once, so you can see everything a formula can do.

A formula with $n$ different letters needs $2^n$ rows. List them in the standard order: the first letter is T for the first half of the rows and F for the second half; each later letter halves the block size; the last letter alternates T, F. Then fill a column for each part, ending with the main connective.

Each letter can be T or F independently. With one letter that gives 2 cases; adding a letter doubles the count, because each old case splits into one with the new letter T and one with it F. So 2 letters give 4 rows, 3 give 8, and 4 give 16. The standard order is simply a way to write all of them with no repeats and no gaps.

blocks.html: A full truth table (Building a Truth Table) shows every row a formula can be in. Looking at the main column, three things can happen, and each has a name.
A tautology is true in every row. A self-contradiction is false in every row. A contingent statement is true in at least one row and false in at least one row.

Tautologies are true because of their form alone. $p \lor \neg p$ is true whatever $p$ says, since one of the two disjuncts must be true. Self-contradictions are false by form alone. Contingent statements depend on the facts: whether $p \to q$ is true depends on what $p$ and $q$ say about the world. Logic cannot settle a contingent statement; it can only show which rows make it true.

blocks.cap: A tautology: the main column is T in every row.

blocks.title: A tautology
blocks.q: Classify $(p \land q) \to p$.
steps: The only way to make a conditional F is a T antecedent with an F consequent.
If $p \land q$ is T, then $p$ is T, so the consequent cannot be F.
So no row is F.

blocks.title: A self-contradiction
blocks.q: Classify $(p \to q) \land (p \land \neg q)$.
steps: $p \land \neg q$ is T only in the row $p$ T, $q$ F.
In that row $p \to q$ is F, so the conjunction is F.
In every other row $p \land \neg q$ is F, so the conjunction is F.

blocks.title: Contingent
blocks.q: Classify $(p \lor q) \to p$.
steps: Row $p$ T, $q$ T: T → T is T.
Row $p$ F, $q$ T: T → F is F.
It has a T and an F.

blocks.html: Calling a formula a tautology after checking a few rows. One F anywhere means it is not a tautology, and that row might be the last one you check. Fill the whole column. A shortcut that is safe: to show a formula is not a tautology, one F row is enough; to show it is one, every row must be checked (or you need an argument that no row can be F, as in the first example).

Tautologies matter beyond this lesson. An argument is valid exactly when the conditional "if all the premises, then the conclusion" is a tautology, so every valid argument hides a tautology inside it. And a formula is a self-contradiction exactly when its negation is a tautology, so checking one kind is the same work as checking the other.

blocks.html: Two formulas can look different and still say the same thing. Truth tables (Tautologies, Contradictions and Contingent Statements) let us make that precise.
Two formulas are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of a joint truth table. Then their biconditional is a tautology.

A formula's meaning, as far as logic is concerned, is its column: the rows where it is true. If two formulas have identical columns, there is no situation in which one is true and the other false, so either one can stand in for the other in any argument. That is also exactly when $A \leftrightarrow B$ is true in every row, since a biconditional is true when the sides match.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Equivalent: the two main columns match in every row.

blocks.title: Conditional and disjunction
blocks.q: Are $p \to q$ and $\neg p \lor q$ equivalent?
steps: Column for $p \to q$: T, F, T, T.
Column for $\neg p \lor q$: $\neg p$ is F, F, T, T, so the disjunction is T, F, T, T.
The columns match.

blocks.title: A look-alike that is not
blocks.q: Are $(p \land q) \to r$ and $(p \to q) \to r$ equivalent?
steps: Try the row $p$ F, $q$ F, $r$ F.
$(p \land q) \to r$: F → F is T.
$(p \to q) \to r$: $p \to q$ is T, and T → F is F.
blocks.a: Not equivalent: they differ in that row.

blocks.title: Use the biconditional
blocks.q: How could you test the first example with one column?
steps: Build $(p \to q) \leftrightarrow (\neg p \lor q)$.
If it is T in every row, the two are equivalent.
blocks.a: It is a tautology, so they are equivalent.

blocks.title: Two ways to say if and only if
blocks.q: Are $p \leftrightarrow q$ and $(p \land q) \lor (\neg p \land \neg q)$ equivalent?
steps: $p \leftrightarrow q$ is T when the values match: rows TT and FF.
$(p \land q) \lor (\neg p \land \neg q)$ is T when both are T or both are F: the same two rows.
Both are F in the other two rows.

blocks.html: Notice the difference between being equivalent and merely having the same value in one row. In the row where $p$ and $q$ are both true, $p \land q$ and $p \lor q$ are both T, but they are not equivalent: in the row $p$ T, $q$ F they differ. Equivalence is a claim about every row.

Comparing only the rows where the formulas are true, or deciding by how alike they look. Two formulas can share every T row and still differ where one is F and the other T only if you skipped rows; check every row, T and F alike. And look-alikes are often not equivalent: $(p \land q) \to r$ and $(p \to q) \to r$ differ, as the second example shows.

Equivalences are the raw material of the rules of replacement later in the course (Rules of Replacement). Each of those rules is a pair of equivalent forms, checked once by a truth table and then used anywhere.

blocks.html: There is a neat pattern in the table: the inverse is the contrapositive of the converse. Swap $q \to p$ and negate both parts and you get $\neg p \to \neg q$. That is why the converse and the inverse always agree with each other, while the original and the contrapositive agree with each other.

The contrapositive is useful in proofs. When $p \to q$ is hard to show directly, showing $\neg q \to \neg p$ proves the same thing. Later this becomes a rule of replacement, Transposition (Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl)).

blocks.html: Truth tables compare more than single formulas. With a joint table (Tautologies, Contradictions and Contingent Statements) you can ask how two or more statements relate to each other: can they all be true at once, and can they all be false at once?
Statements are consistent if at least one row makes all of them true; otherwise they are inconsistent. Two statements are contradictory if they have opposite values in every row.

Consistency is about whether a set of claims could describe one possible situation. If no row makes them all true, then believing all of them is a mistake, whatever the facts are. Contradictories are a special, tighter case: exactly one of the pair is true in every row, so they can be neither both true nor both false. Inconsistent statements that are not contradictory can still both be false together.

blocks.html: Calling any two statements that "disagree" contradictory. "The box is all red" and "the box is all blue" cannot both be true, but both are false if the box is green. They are inconsistent, not contradictory. Contradictories must split every row: one T, the other F.

blocks.html: Consistency and validity are linked. An argument is valid exactly when its premises together with the negation of its conclusion are inconsistent: no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false. So a consistency check is another way to test an argument.

Why care? A set of claims that is inconsistent cannot all be true, so if someone asserts all of them, at least one claim must go. That makes consistency a first test for any story, plan or set of beliefs, before anyone checks the facts.

blocks.html: In Validity you learned that an argument is valid when it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Truth tables turn "impossible" into something you can check: every possible situation is a row.
An argument is valid when no row of its truth table makes every premise true and the conclusion false. A row that does is a counterexample, and one counterexample makes the argument invalid.

Each row is one way the world could be, as far as the letters go. "Impossible to have true premises and a false conclusion" means "no row has true premises and a false conclusion". So we write a column for each premise and for the conclusion, and look only at the rows where every premise is true. If the conclusion is true in all of those, the argument is valid.

steps: Rows with both premises T: $\neg p$ needs $p$ F; then $p \lor q$ needs $q$ T.
That is the row $p$ F, $q$ T, where the conclusion $q$ is T.

steps: Rows with both premises T: $p$ T, $q$ T; and $p$ F, $q$ T.

blocks.a: Invalid; the counterexample is $p$ F, $q$ T.

Then $p \to q$ needs $q$ T, but $q \to r$ needs $q$ F.

blocks.html: Looking for a row where everything is true and calling the argument valid, or calling it invalid because some row has a false premise. Rows with a false premise say nothing either way. Only rows where all the premises are true matter, and in those the conclusion must be true.

Remember from Validity and Truth Together that validity is not truth. A valid argument can have a false conclusion when a premise is false, and an invalid argument can have all true statements. The truth table looks at every row, the actual one and all the others, which is exactly why it tests form and not facts.

The table also tells you more than yes or no. When an argument is invalid, the counterexample row describes a concrete situation that breaks it, which is often the most convincing way to show someone the reasoning fails.

blocks.html: A full table for four letters has 16 rows, and for five letters 32. The short truth table method skips most of them. It works backward from the one thing a counterexample must have, as defined in Validity by Truth Table.

Assume every premise true and the conclusion false. Write down the values those assumptions force, one at a time. If you reach a letter that must be both T and F, no counterexample exists and the argument is valid. If you can finish a consistent assignment, it is a counterexample and the argument is invalid.

A counterexample is a row with true premises and a false conclusion. Instead of searching all rows for one, we suppose one exists and see what it would have to look like. Each connective forces values: a false conditional forces T → F, a false disjunction forces both parts F, a true conjunction forces both parts T. If the forced values clash, the supposed row cannot exist.

blocks.html: A form is valid when every argument of that shape is valid, whatever statements the letters stand for. To name an argument's form, check which part of the conditional the second premise matches: the antecedent or the consequent, affirmed or denied.

Validity depends only on form. In modus ponens, the only row with $p \to q$ and $p$ both T has $q$ T, so there is no counterexample, and that stays true whatever $p$ and $q$ mean. Affirming the consequent has a counterexample row ($p$ F, $q$ T), so some argument of that shape has true premises and a false conclusion. That is why we can call the whole form invalid.

blocks.html: Truth tables decide validity, but they grow fast: an argument with six letters needs 64 rows, and predicate logic, later in the course, cannot be handled by tables at all. A proof takes another road. Instead of checking every situation, it shows the conclusion follows by small steps, each one an instance of a form you already know is valid (Valid and Invalid Argument Forms).

A formal proof is a numbered list of lines. The first lines are the premises. Every later line follows from earlier lines by a rule, and the rule and the line numbers it uses are written beside it, like "MP 1, 3". The proof is finished when its last line is the conclusion.

Each rule is a valid argument form. If the premises are true, a line made from true lines by a valid form must be true too, so truth passes down the proof line by line all the way to the conclusion. That is why a correct proof guarantees validity without a single truth table, and why every line must name the rule that justifies it: an unjustified line could break the chain.

blocks.html: Thinking a proof must use every premise, or must be the shortest one. A proof is any chain of correctly justified lines that ends in the conclusion. Extra premises do no harm, and a long correct proof is still a proof. What does matter is that every line has a rule that really fits it.
In the next lessons you will learn the eight rules of inference one or two at a time, starting with modus ponens and modus tollens. Each comes with a pattern to match against whole lines.

blocks.html: MP: from a conditional and its antecedent, infer its consequent. MT: from a conditional and the negation of its consequent, infer the negation of its antecedent. Each cites two lines.

MP is valid because the only row that makes $p \to q$ true and $p$ true also makes $q$ true. MT is valid because if $q$ is false and $p \to q$ is true, $p$ cannot be true (that would make the conditional T → F). Because these are forms, $p$ and $q$ can be replaced by any formulas: from $(r \land s) \to \neg t$ and $r \land s$, MP gives $\neg t$.

What matters is that one cited line is a conditional and the other is exactly its antecedent (for MP) or exactly the negation of its consequent (for MT). "Exactly" means the very same formula, not one that merely says the same thing.
Most proofs you will meet use MP somewhere. When you see a conditional among the premises, ask at once: do I have, or can I get, its antecedent (for MP) or the negation of its consequent (for MT)?

blocks.html: Two more rules of inference come from the valid forms in Valid and Invalid Argument Forms: hypothetical syllogism (HS), which chains conditionals, and disjunctive syllogism (DS), which eliminates one side of an "or". They build on Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens (MP, MT).

blocks.cap: Hypothetical and disjunctive syllogism.

blocks.html: HS: two conditionals that share a middle part give the conditional from the first antecedent to the last consequent. DS: a disjunction and the negation of one disjunct give the other disjunct.

HS is valid because if $p$ leads to $q$ and $q$ leads to $r$, then $p$ leads to $r$: a counterexample would need $p$ T and $r$ F, and then $q$ could be neither T (breaking $q \to r$) nor F (breaking $p \to q$). DS is valid because a true disjunction has at least one true disjunct; if one is false, the other must be the true one.

blocks.html: Using DS with an affirmed disjunct: from $p \lor q$ and $p$, inferring $\neg q$. Because "or" is inclusive, both disjuncts may be true; knowing one is true tells you nothing about the other. DS needs the negation of one disjunct. (In Traditional Logic this mistake is called affirming a disjunct.)

DS needs the exact negation. From $

Notice that both rules have two versions or two orders. DS may eliminate either disjunct, the left or the right, and HS may cite its two conditionals in either order. In each case the shapes must still line up: HS needs the middle formula to be exactly the same in both conditionals.
HS and DS often meet in the same proof: DS frees one part of a disjunction, and HS or MP carries it the rest of the way to the conclusion.

blocks.html: Three short rules handle $\land$ and $\lor$ directly. They look almost too simple, but proofs are full of them. They join the rules from Hypothetical and Disjunctive Syllogism (HS, DS).

blocks.cap: Simplification, conjunction and addition.

blocks.html: Simp takes one conjunct out of a conjunction. Conj joins two lines with $\land$. Add joins anything at all to a line with $\lor$. Simp and Add cite one line; Conj cites two.

If $p \land q$ is true, both parts are true, so either one may be written alone (Simp). If $p$ and $q$ are each true, their conjunction is true (Conj). Addition is the surprising one: if $p$ is true, then $p \lor q$ is true whatever $q$ is, because a disjunction needs only one true part. Adding does lose information, but it never takes you from truth to falsehood, and that is all a rule needs.

Simp works only on a whole line whose main connective is $\land$. The opposite worry, that Add feels like cheating, is unfounded: Add is valid, since $p \lor q$ is true in every row where $p$ is.

blocks.html: These rules are also how you take a conjunction apart and put a new one together. A premise like $p \land (q \to r)$ is two premises in one: Simp gives you $p$ and $q \to r$ as separate lines, and then the other rules can use them. At the end, Conj puts the pieces of a conjunctive conclusion back together.
Watch for Add whenever the conclusion contains a letter that appears in no premise: only Add can introduce something new.

blocks.html: The last of the eight rules of inference is constructive dilemma (CD). It reasons by cases: if either of two things happens, and each leads somewhere, then one of the two results follows. It completes the set begun in Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens (MP, MT).

blocks.html: CD: from a conjunction of two conditionals and the disjunction of their antecedents, infer the disjunction of their consequents. In this system the two conditionals must be joined in one line first, usually by Conj.

If $p \lor r$ is true, at least one of $p$, $r$ is true. If $p$ is, then $p \to q$ gives $q$; if $r$ is, then $r \to s$ gives $s$. Either way, at least one of $q$, $s$ is true, so $q \lor s$ is true. That is two uses of MP, one for each case, packed into one rule.

blocks.html: Using CD with the two conditionals on separate lines. CD cites exactly two lines: the conjunction of the conditionals and the disjunction. With $p \to q$ on line 1 and $r \to s$ on line 2, first write $(p \to q) \land (r \to s)$ by Conj 1, 2, then apply CD. Also check that the disjunction joins the antecedents, not the consequents.

Why bother with CD when two uses of MP would do? Because MP needs the antecedent itself, and in a dilemma you do not know which antecedent is true, only that one of them is. CD is exactly the rule for that situation: reasoning by cases when the cases come as a disjunction.

Some textbooks also have a destructive dilemma (from the conditionals and $

eg r$). Our system leaves it out; you can get the same result with other rules.

CD finishes the list of rules of inference: MP, MT, HS, DS, CD, Simp, Conj and Add. All eight share one restriction, which the next lesson, Matching a Rule to Whole Lines, makes precise: they apply only to whole lines.

blocks.html: Each rule of inference is a pattern written with $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$. In a real proof, those letters stand for whatever formulas fill their places. This lesson makes the matching exact, using the rules from Constructive Dilemma (CD).

A rule of inference applies to whole lines whose main connectives fit the rule's pattern, with any formulas in place of $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$ (the same formula wherever the same letter appears). It never applies to a part of a line.

Validity depends only on form, so if MP is valid for letters, it is valid for any formulas put in place of those letters: the truth table for the bigger argument has the same pattern of T and F in the columns that matter. But a part of a line is not asserted on its own. In $(p \to q) \lor r$, the conditional $p \to q$ might be false (when $r$ is true), so using it as if it were a premise could take you from truths to a falsehood.

A useful habit is to draw an imaginary box around each big part. In $(p \lor q) \to (r \land \neg s)$ the antecedent $p \lor q$ is one box and the consequent $r \land \neg s$ another; the line is then just box $\to$ box, and MP or MT can see it plainly. The rules never look inside a box; they only check how the boxes are joined.

blocks.html: Before you build proofs, practice reading them. Given a finished proof with the justifications removed, you can supply each one by matching the line against the rules of Matching a Rule to Whole Lines.

To justify a line, find the earlier lines it came from, then name the rule whose pattern takes those lines to this one. Write the rule and the line numbers, like "DS 2, 4". The cited lines must come before the line you are justifying.

A justification is a claim that can be checked: "this line follows from those lines by that rule". Writing it forces you to look at the main connectives, which is the habit every proof needs. It also lets someone else check your proof one line at a time without redoing your thinking.

blocks.html: Now you build proofs yourself. You know the eight rules of inference and how to justify a line (Justifying Proof Lines). The question is which line to write next.
Keep the conclusion in view. Look for it inside the premises, then ask which rule could produce it and what that rule needs. Write only lines that move you toward the conclusion.

From any set of premises you could derive endless lines: by Add alone, $p \lor q$, $p \lor r$, $(p \lor q) \lor s$ and so on. Most are useless. A proof is a search, and the conclusion tells you where to search. If the conclusion is the consequent of a premise, you need that premise's antecedent; if it is a conjunct, you need the conjunction; if it is a disjunct, you need the negation of the other disjunct.

It also helps to read the premises once before writing anything. Mark which ones are conditionals (they want MP or MT), which are disjunctions (DS or CD), and which are conjunctions (Simp). Often the shapes alone show the path: a conjunction gets split, its parts feed a conditional, and the result is the conclusion.

blocks.html: Building Short Proofs gave the main idea: work backward from the conclusion. This lesson turns it into a short checklist, with the cases that trip people up most.

Find the conclusion, or its letters, inside the premises. Plan the last step first: which rule would produce the conclusion, and what does it need? Then treat that need as a new goal. When the conclusion contains a letter that appears in no premise, Add is almost always how it gets in.

Working forward, the number of possible lines grows quickly; working backward, each step narrows the search to what one rule needs. It is like planning a trip from the destination: to arrive by train, you must first reach the station. Each premise is a resource; the conclusion tells you which resources to spend.

If a premise mentions it inside a conditional, the other side of that conditional becomes your next goal. If none mentions it at all, look for Add. If two premises mention it, try each; one of the routes usually comes out shorter.

Never using Add, because it seems to lose information. When the conclusion has a letter that no premise has, no other rule can produce it. Look for that clue first: it tells you the last step at once.

blocks.html: The eight rules of inference are not enough on their own. From $ eg (p \land q)$ and $p$ you should be able to get $ eg q$, but no rule of inference fits: the first premise is a negation, not a disjunction. What you need is a way to rewrite $ eg (p \land q)$ as the equivalent $ eg p \lor eg q$ (De Morgan's Laws). That is what rules of replacement do.

A rule of replacement says two forms are logically equivalent, written with "::" between them. Either form may replace the other anywhere, even inside a line, and in either direction. A rule of inference, by contrast, works only on whole lines and only in one direction.

If two formulas are equivalent, they have the same truth value in every row. Swapping one for the other inside a larger formula therefore never changes the value of the larger formula either: the connectives around it see exactly the same truth value as before. That is why replacement may happen inside a line. Inference rules have no such guarantee: $p \land q$ implies $p$, but $p$ does not imply $p \land q$, and replacing one with the other inside $(p \land q) \to r$ could turn a truth into a falsehood.

Before you apply a rule, ask which kind it is. If it has "::", it may go anywhere; if it says "infer", it needs whole lines.

blocks.html: The first two rules of replacement are De Morgan's rule (DM) and double negation (DN). You know both equivalences already from De Morgan's Laws; now they become steps in a proof. They are the rules from Rules of Replacement you will use most.

head: Rule
Form
Form
blocks.cap: Each row: the two forms may replace each other anywhere.

blocks.html: DM moves a negation into or out of a conjunction or disjunction, switching the connective. DN adds or removes two negations in front of the same formula. Both may be used on any part of a line, in either direction, one application per line.

Both pairs are equivalent by truth table, so either form can stand in for the other. DN is the quiet helper: rules like MT and DS need an exact negation, and DN supplies it. From $p o eg q$ and $q$, MT needs $ eg eg q$, the negation of the consequent $ eg q$, and DN turns $q$ into $ eg eg q$.

Moving the negation inside but keeping the connective: writing $

eg p \lor 
eg q$. That is not DM; it changes the meaning (check the row $p$ T, $q$ F). DM always switches $\land$ and $\lor$. A second slip: using DN on two negations that cover different parts, such as turning $

eg p \land q)$ into $p \land q$. The two negations must stand directly in front of the same formula.

When should you reach for DM? Whenever a negation stands in front of parentheses and the next rule needs the parts separately. A negated conjunction becomes a disjunction, which DS can use; a negated disjunction becomes a conjunction, which Simp can take apart. DN is the finishing touch whenever a rule wants $\neg \neg p$ and you have $p$, or the other way round.
Typing tip: in the answer box, ~~p is read as $\neg \neg p$. There is no need for parentheses around a double negation.
Each use of a replacement rule changes one part, once. If a line needs DM in two places, use two lines, each justified "DM" with the line it came from. That keeps every step easy to check.

blocks.html: Three more rules of replacement let you reorder, regroup and spread out conjunctions and disjunctions. With them, together with De Morgan and Double Negation (DM, DN), you can reshape a line until an inference rule fits.

head: Rule
Form
Form
blocks.cap: Commutation, association and distribution.

blocks.html: Com swaps the two sides of $\land$ or $\lor$. Assoc regroups three parts joined by the same connective. Dist spreads $\land$ over $\lor$, or $\lor$ over $\land$, like multiplication over addition.

The order of the parts never matters for $\land$ and $\lor$, since "both" and "at least one" do not care which comes first. Grouping does not matter when all the connectives are the same: "$p$ and $q$ and $r$" means all three, however you bracket them. Dist is the logical version of $a(b + c) = ab + ac$: "$p$, and either $q$ or $r$" is true exactly when "$p$ and $q$" or "$p$ and $r$" is.

blocks.a: Dist turns the premise into a disjunction that DS can use.

blocks.html: Using Com on a conditional (turning $p \to q$ into $q \to p$) or Assoc on mixed connectives (turning $p \land (q \lor r)$ into $(p \land q) \lor r$). Neither is allowed, and both change the meaning: the first is the converse, and the second is false when $p$ is false and $r$ is true. Com and Assoc work only with $\land$ and $\lor$, and Assoc only when all the connectives are the same.

These three rules rarely finish a proof on their own. Their job is to line formulas up. DS, for instance, needs the negation of one disjunct; if the disjunction has three parts, Assoc can group them so that the part you can deny stands alone on one side. Com does the same when a conclusion lists the parts in a different order from the line you have.

A tip for Dist: it is the rule to reach for when a line has $\land$ outside and $\lor$ inside (or the reverse) and you need the other arrangement. Read it in both directions: from $(p \lor q) \land (p \lor r)$ you can pull the common $p$ back out, giving $p \lor (q \land r)$.

blocks.html: Two rules of replacement deal with conditionals. Transposition (Trans) turns a conditional into its contrapositive, which you know is equivalent from Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive. Material implication (Impl) turns a conditional into a disjunction. They extend Commutation, Association and Distribution (Com, Assoc, Dist).

head: Rule
Form
Form
blocks.cap: Transposition and material implication.

blocks.html: Trans: a conditional may be replaced by its contrapositive (swap the parts and negate both), and back. Impl: $p \to q$ may be replaced by $\neg p \lor q$, and back.

Both pairs have the same truth table: $p o q$, $ eg q o eg p$ and $ eg p \lor q$ are each false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. Impl says a conditional amounts to "either the antecedent fails or the consequent holds", which is the promise reading of Truth Values of the Connectives in other words. These rules let you move between conditionals and disjunctions, so MP, MT, DS and HS can all reach the same information.

Impl also explains why $p \lor q$ is equivalent to $ eg p o q$: replace $p$ by $ eg p$ in the rule, giving $ eg p o q$ :: $ eg eg p \lor q$, and DN finishes the job. Translating "unless" as $\lor$ in Translating Conditionals rested on exactly this equivalence.

blocks.html: The last three rules of replacement handle the biconditional, conditionals with conjunctions inside, and repeated parts. With them you have all ten, completing the list begun in Rules of Replacement and continued in Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl).

head: Rule
Form
Form
blocks.cap: Material equivalence, exportation and tautology.

blocks.html: Equiv unpacks a biconditional into two conditionals, or into "both or neither". Exp moves the first conjunct of an antecedent out in front: $(p \land q) \to r$ :: $p \to (q \to r)$. Taut removes or adds a repeated part joined to itself.

A biconditional is true when both sides match, which is exactly when each side implies the other, or when both are true or both are false. Exportation reflects how conditions stack: "if you have a ticket and it is Saturday, you can enter" says the same as "if you have a ticket, then if it is Saturday, you can enter". Taut is obvious once said aloud: "$p$ or $p$" and "$p$ and $p$" both just say $p$.

blocks.html: Exporting into $(p \to q) \to r$. That is not equivalent: the third column above shows rows where $(p \land q) \to r$ is true and $(p \to q) \to r$ is false (for instance $p$ F, $q$ F, $r$ F). Exportation keeps $r$ at the very end and moves only $p$ out in front: $p \to (q \to r)$.

Each of these rules earns its place in proofs. Equiv is the only way to use a biconditional: no rule of inference cites one directly. Exp lets MP reach a consequent when you have the conjuncts of the antecedent on separate lines (with Exp you need only one at a time). Taut tidies up after CD when both conditionals lead to the same place.

items: A biconditional you want to use: Equiv first.
An antecedent that is a conjunction: consider Exp.
A disjunction or conjunction of a formula with itself: Taut.

blocks.html: You now have all eighteen rules: eight of inference (Proof Strategy: Working Backward) and ten of replacement (Equivalence, Exportation and Tautology (Equiv, Exp, Taut)). Real proofs mix them, and the skill is knowing when to reshape a line and when to infer from it.
Use rules of replacement to reshape a line until an inference rule fits; then infer. Before each step, ask what shape the next inference rule needs, and replace only toward that shape.

Inference rules are picky about form: MT needs an exact negated consequent, DS an exact negated disjunct, MP an exact antecedent. Replacement rules are the adapters that make the shapes line up. Working backward tells you which shape you need, so you are not trying all ten rules at random.

blocks.html: Reaching for a long chain of replacements when a short inference would do. Five replacement steps that end where one MT would have taken you are not wrong, but they are easy to get wrong. Plan backward: name the inference rule that will finish the proof, then use the fewest replacements needed to give it the shape it wants.

Two habits help most. First, always look at the main connective of each premise and of the conclusion, since that is all the rules ever see. Second, remember the common adapters: DN for exact negations, DM for negations in front of parentheses, Impl to switch between conditionals and disjunctions, and Equiv to unpack a biconditional. With those four, most proofs fall into place.

blocks.html: Many conclusions are conditionals: $p \to r$, $p \to (q \land r)$. Conditional proof (CP) proves them directly, the way people argue every day: "Suppose $p$. Then … so $r$. So if $p$, then $r$." It extends the rules of Proofs with All Eighteen Rules.

To prove $A \to B$ by CP: assume $A$ on a new line (justified ACP), indented in a subproof. Derive $B$ inside the subproof, using the assumption and any earlier lines. Then close the subproof and write $A \to B$, justified "CP i–j", where $i$ is the assumption line and $j$ the last line of the subproof.

Inside the subproof you have shown: whenever $A$ (and the premises) are true, $B$ is true. That is exactly what $A \to B$ claims, given the premises. The assumption is not a new premise; it is a supposition for the sake of argument. Once the subproof is closed, the assumption is dropped, and only the conditional it produced remains.

blocks.html: Using a line from inside a closed subproof later. Once CP closes the subproof, its lines depended on an assumption that is no longer in force; citing them afterward would let you use the supposition as if it were a fact. After the CP line, only lines outside the subproof (and the new conditional) may be cited.

CP is safe because the assumption cannot leak out. Everything derived inside the box is marked by the indentation as depending on it, and the only thing that leaves the box is a conditional that states that dependence openly. You may open a CP subproof at any time, assuming anything you like; the price is that you must close it before the proof ends.
The assumption may be any formula, not only a letter. To prove $(p \lor q) \to r$, assume $p \lor q$.

blocks.html: Indirect proof (IP), also called proof by contradiction, is the second new method. To show a statement is true, you assume it is false and show that leads to a contradiction. The layout is the same subproof you used in Conditional Proof (CP).

To prove $A$ by IP: assume $
eg A$ (justified AIP) in a subproof. Derive a contradiction, a line of the form $q \land 
eg q$. Close the subproof and write $A$, justified "IP i–j". (If you assumed $B$ instead, IP gives $
eg B$.)

If the premises together with $
eg A$ lead to $q \land 
eg q$, which is false in every row, then the premises and $
eg A$ cannot all be true. So whenever the premises are true, $
eg A$ is false, which means $A$ is true. IP is the formal version of "that can't be right, so the opposite must be".

blocks.html:
Stopping when you reach some line that looks false, such as $
eg p$ when you "know" $p$. The subproof must end in an explicit contradiction of the form $q \land 
eg q$, written on one line. If you have $q$ and $
eg q$ on separate lines, use Conj to put them together before you close.
Any contradiction will do; it need not involve the letters of the conclusion.

Notice how IP differs from CP. CP proves a conditional and gives you something to aim for: the consequent. IP can prove anything, but the target inside the subproof is vaguer: any contradiction at all. A good strategy is to look for a formula and its negation that are both within reach, then aim for each of them.

IP is often the easiest way to prove a negation, or a simple letter that appears only deep inside the premises. When nothing else suggests itself, assume the opposite of the conclusion and look for two lines that clash.

blocks.html: A subproof can contain another subproof. That lets you prove conclusions like $p \to (q \to r)$, where the consequent is itself a conditional, and even prove statements from no premises at all. This builds on Indirect Proof (IP) and Conditional Proof (CP).

Subproofs nest like parentheses: the last one opened is the first one closed. Inside an inner subproof you may cite lines from the outer subproofs that are still open; after a subproof is closed, none of its lines can be cited. A proof must end with every subproof closed.

Each assumption is a supposition that holds only inside its own box. An inner box sits inside the outer one, so both suppositions are in force there. When the inner box closes, its supposition is discharged (turned into the antecedent of a conditional, or denied by IP), but the outer supposition is still on. Closing the outer box first would leave the inner supposition dangling, with nothing to discharge it.

blocks.html: Every formula proved from no premises is a tautology, and every tautology of statement logic can be proved this way.

Why prove theorems at all? A theorem is a logical truth: something that holds whatever the facts are. Proving one from nothing shows that the rules alone produce it, and it confirms the truth table, which would show the same formula is a tautology. Later, in Soundness and Completeness, you will see that this agreement is no accident.

Closing the outer subproof before the inner one, or ending the proof with a subproof still open. Close innermost first, each with CP or IP citing its own range. The last line of the whole proof must stand at the left margin, outside every box; if it does not, it still depends on an assumption and has not been proved.

blocks.html: Statement logic treats "Ava is friendly" as an unbroken block, a single letter $p$. That is fine until an argument depends on what is inside the block. "All dogs are mammals; Rex is a dog; so Rex is a mammal" is valid, but in statement logic it looks like $p$, $q$, so $r$, which is not valid at all. To see why it works we need to look inside simple statements, at the things they are about and what they say of them. This takes up the subject and predicate terms of Categorical Propositions and the simple statements of Simple and Compound Statements.

A predicate letter (a capital: $F$, $D$, $M$) stands for a property: "is friendly", "is a dog". A name (a lowercase letter $a$, $b$, $c$ …) stands for one individual. Write the predicate first, then the name: $Fa$ says that $a$ is $F$.

Splitting a sentence into predicate and name lets two sentences share parts. "Rex is a dog" and "Rex is a mammal" become $Dr$ and $Mr$: they mention the same individual $r$, and that shared name is what lets the argument connect. Statement letters hid that connection. All the connectives still work exactly as before: $Fa \land \neg Ta$, $Fa \to Fb$ and so on.

blocks.html: Names let us talk about particular things (Predicates and Names). Quantifiers let us talk about all things, or some, without naming them. That is what "All dogs are mammals" and "Some birds cannot fly" need.

$\forall x Fx$ (read "for all $x$, $x$ is $F$") says everything is $F$. $\exists x Fx$ ("there is an $x$ such that $x$ is $F$") says at least one thing is $F$. A variable like $x$ is bound when a quantifier covers it.

A variable is a placeholder, like a pronoun: $Fx$ alone says "it is $F$" without saying what "it" is, so it is neither true nor false. A quantifier fixes how to read the placeholder: $\forall x$ means "whatever you pick", $\exists x$ means "for at least one choice". The domain, the collection of things we are talking about, is fixed in advance: people in a club, shapes in a picture.

steps: Deny the universal: $\neg \forall x Lx$.

blocks.html: Any variable will do: $\forall x Rx$ and $\forall y Ry$ say exactly the same thing, since the variable only marks which places the quantifier governs. We use $x$, $y$ and $z$ for variables and keep $a$, $b$, $c$ for names, so a reader can always tell a placeholder from a particular object.

Watch the scope of a quantifier: it covers only what comes right after it. In $\exists x Fx \land Gx$ the $\exists x$ covers only $Fx$, and the $x$ in $Gx$ is left free, so the formula is not a complete sentence. Use parentheses, $\exists x(Fx \land Gx)$, to make the quantifier cover both.

blocks.html: Universal statements (A and E) use $\forall$ with $\to$: "for anything, if it is an $S$, then …". Particular statements (I and O) use $\exists$ with $\land$: "there is something that is an $S$ and …".

"All dogs are mammals" is not about everything being a dog; it says that anything which is a dog is a mammal. That "if" is the arrow. "Some dogs are pets" says there is a thing that is both a dog and a pet; that "both" is the $\land$. Swapping them gives nonsense: $\forall x(Dx \land Mx)$ says everything in the domain is a dog and a mammal, and $\exists x(Dx \to Px)$ is true as soon as one thing in the domain is not a dog, since a conditional with a false antecedent is true.

blocks.title: An A statement
blocks.q: Let $Wx$: $x$ is a whale; $Mx$: $x$ is a mammal. Translate "Every whale is a mammal."
steps: Universal, affirmative: $\forall$ with $\to$.

blocks.title: An O statement in disguise
blocks.q: Translate "Not every whale is a fish" ($Fx$: $x$ is a fish).
steps: "Not every" denies an A statement: $\neg \forall x(Wx \to Fx)$.
That is equivalent to an O statement: some whale is not a fish.

blocks.title: An E statement
blocks.q: Translate "No reptiles are pets" ($Lx$: reptile; $Px$: pet).
steps: For anything, if it is a reptile, it is not a pet.

blocks.html: Pairing $\forall$ with $\land$ or $\exists$ with $\to$. $\forall x(Sx \land Px)$ says everything is both $S$ and $P$, which is far too strong. $\exists x(Sx \to Px)$ is far too weak: it is true if anything at all is not an $S$. Memorize the pairs: all goes with if, some goes with and.

English offers many ways to say each form. "Every", "each" and "any" usually mark an A statement; "no" and "not a single" an E statement; "some", "there is" and "at least one" an I statement; "not every" and "not all" an O statement. Decide which of the four forms the sentence expresses before you write any symbols, and the pairing of quantifier and connective follows.
Predicate logic reads A and E statements without existential import: $\forall x(Sx \to Px)$ is true when there are no $S$ at all. That is the modern reading taught in Existential Import.

blocks.html: Translate the subject phrase into one condition (an adjective adds $\land$) and the predicate phrase into another, then join them with $\to$ under $\forall$ or $\land$ under $\exists$. "Only $S$ are $P$" reverses the order: $\forall x(Px \to Sx)$.

"Only members may vote" does not say every member votes; it says anyone who votes is a member. The word after "only" names a necessary condition, and a necessary condition goes after the arrow, just as with "only if" in Translating Conditionals. "Cats and dogs are pets" uses "and" in English, but no single thing is both a cat and a dog; the sentence means anything that is a cat or a dog is a pet.

A handy pattern from these examples: once the negation has moved inside, a universal statement usually ends with an arrow inside it and an existential one with an "and". If your result has $\exists x(\ldots \to \ldots)$ or $\forall x(\ldots \land \ldots)$, look again; it is probably a slip.

In proofs, QN is a rule of replacement: it may be used on any part of a line, in either direction. It is often the first step when a premise begins with a negation, because the instantiation rules of the next unit need a quantifier in front.

blocks.html: Truth tables decided truth in statement logic. In predicate logic the role of a row is played by a world: a domain of objects, with each predicate true of some of them. Here you evaluate quantified sentences (Quantifier Negation) in small worlds you can see.

A universal sentence such as $\forall x(Fx \to Gx)$ is true in a world when its inside holds for every object in the domain; one counterexample makes it false. An existential sentence such as $\exists x(Fx \land Gx)$ is true when its inside holds for at least one object, a witness. Evaluate the inside by testing each object in turn.

A quantified sentence makes a claim about the whole domain, so its truth depends on which objects exist and what they are like. Change the world and the truth value can change; that is why the same sentence can be true here and false there. A small world lets you check every object by eye, which is exactly what the definitions ask for.

$a$ is a circle.

blocks.html: Checking only the objects that make a universal conditional "about something". For $\forall x(Lx \to Cx)$, the small objects pass automatically, since their antecedent is false. And for an existential, one witness is enough; you do not need all objects to pass.

blocks.html: One more point about domains: the same sentence can be true in one world and false in another, but in a single world it has exactly one truth value. That is what makes a world work like a row of a truth table, and why the next lesson can use worlds as counterexamples.

items: $\forall$: check every object; stop at the first counterexample.
$\exists$: look for one witness; stop when you find it.
Inside the quantifier, use the connectives' truth tables as usual.

blocks.html: In statement logic, a counterexample to an argument is a row with true premises and a false conclusion (Validity by Truth Table). In predicate logic it is a world with true premises and a false conclusion. Building one is how you show a predicate argument is invalid, using what you learned in Truth in a Small World.
A predicate-logic argument is invalid when some world makes every premise true and the conclusion false. To show invalidity, build such a world, then check each premise and the conclusion in it.

Validity means no possible situation has true premises and a false conclusion. A world is one possible situation, so a single counterexample world settles invalidity. (Showing validity needs a proof, the topic of the next unit, since there are infinitely many worlds to rule out.) Small worlds with two or three objects are usually enough to break an invalid argument.

World: one object $a$ that is $G$ and not $F$.
Premise: true (there are no $F$ to fail). Conclusion: false ($a$ is $G$ but not $F$).
blocks.a: Invalid: the one-object world is a counterexample.

steps: World: $a$ is $F$ only; $b$ is $G$ only.
Both premises are true; nothing is both, so the conclusion is false.

items: Make the conclusion false first: that usually fixes a lot.
Then add or adjust objects until each premise is true.
Check everything again at the end.

blocks.html: Sometimes no world works, however hard you try. That is a hint, though not a proof, that the argument is valid. The next unit gives the tools to prove it: rules that let you reason from quantified premises directly.
Counterexample worlds are the predicate-logic twin of the short truth table method: start from what the counterexample needs and fill in the rest.

blocks.html: Worlds can show that a predicate argument is invalid (Counterexample Worlds), but to show validity we need proofs. The plan is simple: take the quantifiers off, reason with the eighteen rules you already know (Proofs with All Eighteen Rules), and put quantifiers back on at the end. This lesson gives the two easiest quantifier rules, universal instantiation and existential generalization, and uses Quantifier Negation when a premise starts with a negation.

blocks.cap: The letters stand for any formulas: from $\forall x(Fx \to Gx)$, UI gives $Fa \to Ga$.

blocks.html: UI: from a universal statement, drop the $\forall x$ and put one name (or variable) for every $x$ it covered. EG: from a statement about a name, replace that name (in some or all of its places) with a variable and put $\exists$ in front of the whole line. Both apply only to whole lines.

If something holds for everything, it holds for Ava, for Ben, for any particular thing you choose: that is UI. If something holds for Ava, then it holds for at least one thing: that is EG. Both are plainly truth-preserving. With them, "All dogs are mammals; Rex is a dog; so Rex is a mammal" becomes a three-line proof.

blocks.html: Applying UI to part of a line, such as $\forall x Fx \to Ga$. Its main connective is $\to$, not $\forall$: the quantifier covers only $Fx$. Like the rules of inference, the quantifier rules act only on whole lines whose main connective is the quantifier. If a line begins with $\neg Ax$, use QN first to get a quantifier in front.

Choosing the name for UI is up to you, so choose with the goal in mind. If the conclusion or another premise mentions $c$, instantiate with $c$, because that is the object the argument is about. Instantiating a universal premise with a name nobody mentions is legal but rarely gets you anywhere.

EG: a name → a variable under $\exists$, covering the whole line.
Never: UI on a part of a line, or EG giving $\forall$.

blocks.html: Existential instantiation (EI) takes the quantifier off an existential statement. It is the one rule with a real catch, and the catch is about names. It joins UI and EG from Universal Instantiation and Existential Generalization (UI, EG).
EI: from $\exists x Fx$, infer $Fa$ for a name $a$ that is new: it appears in no earlier line, no premise and not in the conclusion.

$\exists x Fx$ says something is $F$, but not which thing. EI gives that unknown thing a temporary name. The name must be new because we know nothing else about the thing. If $a$ already appeared, say in $Ga$, then writing $Fa$ would claim that the $F$ thing is the same as the $G$ thing, which the premises never said. A fresh name carries no information except what $\exists x Fx$ provides.

UI may use any name, including a.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.q: Premises $\forall x(Fx \to Gx)$ and $\exists x Fx$. Why use EI before UI?

EI needs a new name, so if UI goes first with $a$, EI cannot use $a$ any more.
blocks.a: Do EI first, then UI with the same name.

blocks.html: Reusing a name: from $\exists x Fx$ and $\exists x Gx$, writing $Fa$ and then $Ga$, as if the same thing had both properties. Then $\exists x(Fx \land Gx)$ would seem to follow, but it does not: one person may be a doctor and another a pilot without anyone being both. Before every EI, scan the lines above and the conclusion for the name you plan to use.

Notice that EI, unlike UI, can be used only once per existential line in a useful way: every later use would need yet another new name, and each name would stand for a possibly different thing. That is the honest bookkeeping the rule enforces.

The strategy that follows from this rule is one of the most useful in predicate proofs: EI before UI. Instantiate the existential premises first, each with its own new name, then instantiate the universal premises with those same names.

The name EI introduces must not appear in the conclusion either. A conclusion like $Fa$ cannot be reached by instantiating $\exists x Fx$ to $a$: knowing that something is $F$ does not show that $a$ in particular is.

blocks.html: Universal generalization (UG) puts a $\forall$ back on. It is how you prove a conclusion like $\forall x(Fx \to Hx)$. Like EI (Existential Instantiation (EI)), it has a restriction, and the restriction is the whole point of the rule.

UG: from $Fy$, infer $\forall x Fx$, but only when $y$ is a variable that stands for any object: it came from UI, it is not a name, it was not introduced by EI, and it is not free in an assumption that is still open.

To show everything is $F$, it is enough to show that an arbitrary thing is $F$: one about which you assumed nothing special. A variable produced by UI is exactly that, since UI works for anything at all. A name like $a$ is different: proving $Fa$ shows only that one thing is $F$. A name from EI is the most special of all: it names the very thing that has some property. Generalizing from either would leap from "one" to "all".

blocks.html: Generalizing from a particular name: from $Fa$, writing $\forall x Fx$. Showing one object is $F$ does not show every object is. When you plan to use UG at the end of a proof, use UI with a variable ($y$, $z$) from the start, not a name.

A familiar comparison: a geometry teacher proves a fact about "any triangle" by drawing one triangle and using only what holds for every triangle. That drawn triangle plays the role of $y$. If the proof used something special about it, such as its being isosceles, the conclusion would hold only for triangles like it.

Check that the variable did not come from EI and is not in an open assumption.
Generalize: put $\forall x$ in front and $x$ for the variable everywhere.

blocks.html: UI and UG work as a pair: UI takes a universal claim down to an arbitrary object, the propositional rules work on it, and UG lifts the result back to a universal claim. EI and EG are the other pair, for existential claims.

blocks.html: You now have all four quantifier rules (UI, EG, EI, UG) and quantifier negation (QN). This lesson puts them together into a strategy for predicate proofs, building on Universal Generalization (UG).
Strip the quantifiers (use QN first if a premise starts with a negation; then EI before UI), reason with the propositional rules, then put quantifiers back with EG or UG as the conclusion requires.

Once the quantifiers are off, the lines are just like statement logic: $Fa \to Ga$ behaves like $p \to q$. So all the proof skills of the earlier units carry over. The quantifier rules are the doors in and out. Their restrictions decide the order: EI needs a fresh name, so it goes first; UG needs an arbitrary variable, so plan for it from the start.

Why does the second example use variables instead of names? Because the conclusion is universal and must end with UG, which only works on a variable. Had line 3 been $Fa$, the proof would reach $Fa \land Ga$ and then be stuck, since UG never applies to a name.

blocks.html: Conditional and indirect proof (Nested Subproofs) work in predicate logic too. Combined with the quantifier rules of Proofs with Quantifiers, they prove conclusions that are conditionals or negations, and they often make long proofs short.

Use CP to prove a conditional (assume its antecedent) and IP to prove anything by assuming its negation, exactly as before. The quantifier rules keep their restrictions inside subproofs, plus one more: UG may not generalize a variable that is free in an assumption that is still open.

Inside a subproof that assumes $Fy$, the variable $y$ is no longer arbitrary: it stands for something assumed to be $F$. Generalizing there would turn "if $y$ is $F$, then …" into a claim about everything, which proves too much. Once the subproof is closed, the assumption has become the antecedent of a conditional, and the variable is arbitrary again, so UG is safe after the CP line.

blocks.title: IP with quantifiers
blocks.q: Premises $\forall x(Fx \to Gx)$ and $\neg \exists x Gx$. Prove $\neg \exists x Fx$.
steps: Assume $\exists x Fx$ (AIP). EI: $Fa$.
UI: $Fa \to Ga$. MP: $Ga$.
QN on premise 2: $\forall x\neg Gx$. UI: $\neg Ga$.
Conj: $Ga \land \neg Ga$. IP: $\neg \exists x Fx$.
blocks.a: The assumption leads to a contradiction.

blocks.html: Using UG inside a subproof on a variable that is free in the assumption. If line 2 assumes $Fy$, then inside that subproof you may not write $\forall x Gx$ from $Gy$: that would claim everything is $G$ just because the one assumed $F$ thing is. Close the subproof with CP first, then generalize the conditional.

The extra restriction on UG is the only new thing in this lesson. Everything else is the same CP and IP you already know, with quantifier steps inside. It helps to mark, as you go, which variables appear in each open assumption; those are the ones UG must leave alone until the box closes.
EI inside a subproof still needs a new name, one that appears nowhere above it, including in the assumption.
IP is especially handy in predicate logic when the conclusion is a negated quantifier, like $\neg \exists x Fx$: assume the quantifier without the negation, instantiate it, and look for a clash.
