blocks.html: So far every predicate has said something about one thing: $Fa$. Many claims link two or more things: "Ava helps Ben", "7 is greater than 3", "the library is between the park and the school". Relational predicates handle them. They extend the translations of Translating Harder Quantified Sentences.

A relational predicate has two or more places, filled in order. $Hab$ says $a$ helps $b$; $Hba$ says $b$ helps $a$. The order of the names is part of the meaning, and quantifiers can fill any of the places: $\forall x Hxb$ (everyone helps Ben), $\exists x Hbx$ (Ben helps someone).

"Ava helps Ben" and "Ben helps Ava" are different facts: one can be true while the other is false. A one-place predicate cannot express that difference, since $Ha \land Hb$ says only that both are helpers. With a two-place predicate the order of the names records who does what to whom. That is also why many valid arguments, like "Ava is taller than Ben; Ben is taller than Cleo; so Ava is taller than Cleo" (with the right premise about "taller"), need relations at all.

When you set up a predicate, write its meaning with variables in order, like "$Hxy$: $x$ helps $y$", and then fill the places in exactly that order. Passive sentences reverse the English order: "Ben is helped by Ava" is still $Hab$.

blocks.html: Relations can have more than two places. "The library is between the park and the school" uses a three-place predicate: $Blps$, with the order fixed by the key "$Bxyz$: $x$ is between $y$ and $z$". The same care applies: decide the order of the places once, write it down, and stick to it.
Relations with quantifiers in two places, like "everyone likes someone", need two quantifiers, and their order turns out to matter a great deal. That is the next lesson.

blocks.html: With relations (Relational Predicates) a sentence can have two quantifiers, and then their order matters. "Everyone likes someone" and "someone is liked by everyone" sound alike but say very different things. Use what you learned in Truth in a Small World to check them in small worlds.

Read quantifiers from left to right. $\forall x\exists y Lxy$: for each person $x$ there is some $y$ that $x$ likes (each may like a different person). $\exists y\forall x Lxy$: there is one person $y$ whom every $x$ likes. The second implies the first, but not the other way round.

In $\forall x\exists y Lxy$, the choice of $y$ comes after $x$ is fixed, so $y$ may depend on $x$: Ava likes Ben, Ben likes Cleo, Cleo likes Ava, and everyone likes someone. In $\exists y\forall x Lxy$, $y$ is chosen first, once, and must work for every $x$. That is a much stronger claim: one person liked by all. If such a person exists, then of course everyone likes someone (that person), which is why one direction is valid.

blocks.html: Treating $\forall x Ey$ and $\exists y Ax$ as the same. The first lets each $x$ pick its own $y$; the second needs one $y$ for all. A quick test: a circle of three people, each liking the next, makes the first true and the second false. When translating, keep the order of "everyone" and "someone" exactly as the English has it, and read the formula back to check.

items: Same quantifiers can swap: $\forall x\forall y Lxy$ means the same as $\forall y\forall x Lxy$, and $\exists x Ey$ as $\exists y Ex$.
Mixed quantifiers cannot swap.
$\exists y\forall x Lxy$ implies $\forall x\exists y Lxy$; the converse fails.

blocks.html: How do you evaluate a sentence with two quantifiers in a world? Peel them one at a time. For $\forall x\exists y Lxy$, go through each person $x$ and ask whether $\exists y Lxy$ holds for that $x$: is there an arrow leaving $x$? For $\exists y\forall x Lxy$, go through each candidate $y$ and ask whether every $x$ has an arrow into it. The outer quantifier tells you which question to repeat.
Quantifier order is one of the places where symbols beat English. "Every student read a book" can mean each read some book or all read the same book; the formulas force you to say which.

blocks.html: Some relations behave in regular ways: "is the same age as" always holds both ways, and "is older than" passes along a chain. These patterns have names, and they are written with the quantifiers of Quantifier Order.

blocks.cap: Three properties of a relation $R$.

blocks.html: A relation is reflexive if everything bears it to itself, symmetric if whenever it holds one way it holds the other way, and transitive if whenever it holds from $x$ to $y$ and from $y$ to $z$, it holds from $x$ to $z$. A relation can have any combination of these, or none.

These properties are what make some arguments valid. "Ava is taller than Ben, and Ben is taller than Cleo, so Ava is taller than Cleo" is valid only once we add the premise that "taller than" is transitive. Spelling the properties out as formulas lets a proof use them like any other premise.

It is not.

blocks.title: Everyday relations
blocks.q: Which properties does "is a sibling of" have?
steps: Not reflexive: no one is their own sibling.
Symmetric: if Ava is Ben's sibling, Ben is Ava's.
Not transitive: Ava is Ben's sibling and Ben is Ava's, but Ava is not her own sibling.

blocks.html: Thinking that a relation that is not symmetric must be asymmetric (never holding both ways). "Loves" can hold both ways for some pairs and one way for others; then it is neither symmetric nor asymmetric. Failing a property only takes one counterexample pair; having the opposite property needs every pair to fit.

Mathematics is full of these properties. "Equals" is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (a relation with all three is called an equivalence relation). "Is less than" is transitive but neither reflexive nor symmetric. "Divides", on whole numbers, is reflexive and transitive. Checking the three properties is often the first thing a mathematician does with a new relation.

items: To refute a property, find one pair (or triple) that breaks it.
To confirm it, check every pair (or every chain of two arrows).
Loops ($x$ to $x$) matter for reflexivity and can matter for transitivity.

blocks.html: Identity is a special relation: $a = b$ says that $a$ and $b$ are the same object. With it we can say things that were out of reach before, like "only", "someone else" and "the same". It builds on the relations of Relational Predicates.

$a = b$ says the names $a$ and $b$ refer to one and the same object; $a 
e b$ (that is, $a 
e b$) says they refer to different objects. Identity lets us translate "only Ava": $Fa \land  orall x(Fx 	o x = a)$, and "someone other than Ava": $\exists x(Fx \land x 
e a)$.

One object can have two names: "Mark Twain" and "Samuel Clemens" name one writer, and "the morning star" and "the evening star" name one planet. Identity records that. Because there is only one object, whatever is true of it under one name is true of it under the other; that is the idea behind the identity rule in Proofs with Identity. And because $x$ and $a$ can be compared, we can say "anything that is $F$ is Ava", which is what "only Ava is $F$" adds to $Fa$.

blocks.html: Reading $a = b$ as "$a$ and $b$ are alike". Identity is not similarity: twins are alike, but they are two people, so $a \ne b$. $a = b$ says there is only one thing, with two names. A check: if $a = b$, then whatever is true of $a$ must be true of $b$, with no exceptions.

Identity also gives "the" a precise meaning. "The team captain sings" says there is exactly one team captain and that person sings; with identity you can write that out (see At Least, At Most and Exactly). Names already pick out one object each, so with names a plain $a = t$ or $St$ is enough.

Notice the shape of "only Ava sings": it is a conjunction, not a single quantifier. Leaving out $Sa$ would give $\forall x(Sx \to x = a)$, which says nobody but Ava sings but allows that Ava does not sing either. Most uses of "only" with a name need both parts.

blocks.html: Identity (Identity) lets logic count, without any numbers. "At least two", "at most one" and "exactly one" can all be written with quantifiers, $=$ and $\neq$.

head: English
Symbols
blocks.cap: Counting with identity.

blocks.html: "At least two" needs two variables and $x \neq y$ to make them different. "At most one" says any two $F$ things are identical. "Exactly one" is at least one and at most one: something is $F$, and anything $F$ is that thing.

Two variables do not have to name two different things. $\exists x\exists y(Fx \land Fy)$ is true in a world with a single $F$ object: let $x$ and $y$ both be that object. So to say "two", you must say the two are distinct, which is what $x \neq y$ does. In the other direction, "at most one" cannot list the objects; instead it says that whenever you find $F$ things, they turn out to be one and the same.

blocks.html: Writing $\exists x\exists y(Fx \land Fy)$ for "at least two". Without $x \neq y$, both variables can be the same object, so the formula says only "at least one". Whenever you mean "two different things", add the $\neq$.

These formulas can be checked in a world like the one above. For "at least two red shapes", look for two different red objects: $a$ and $b$ will do. For "at most one", look for two different objects with the property; finding them makes the sentence false. For "exactly one", find one and check there is no second.

The pattern extends to any number. "At least three" needs three variables, all pairwise different: $x 
eq y$, $x 
eq z$ and $y 
eq z$. It gets long, but it shows something remarkable: counting, which seems to need numbers, can be done with logic alone.
"At most one" is true when nothing is $F$ at all, since then there are no two $F$ things to compare. That is why "exactly one" adds $\exists x Fx$ to it.

blocks.html: Identity needs its own rule in proofs. You already use identity in translations (At Least, At Most and Exactly); here it joins the quantifier rules (Proofs with Quantifiers) and quantifier order (Quantifier Order) in the proof system.

From

blocks.cap: The identity rule (Id).

blocks.html: Id has three forms: write $a = a$ at any time; turn $a = b$ around into $b = a$; and from a line about $a$ plus $a = b$, replace $a$ by $b$ in some or all places. Every use is justified "Id" with the lines it cites.

Everything is identical to itself, so $a = a$ needs no premise. Identity goes both ways: if $a$ is $b$, then $b$ is $a$. And if $a$ and $b$ are one object, anything true of it under one name is true under the other: if Mark Twain wrote a novel and Mark Twain is Samuel Clemens, then Samuel Clemens wrote a novel. Substitution is that principle written as a rule.

blocks.html: Substituting in the wrong place, or treating $a = b$ as a premise about a property. Id replaces a name by another name for the same object, inside a line you already have; it never changes a predicate letter, and $a = b$ is not a fact about $a$'s qualities. A check: the new line must be exactly the old one with some occurrences of one name swapped for the other.

Identity proofs often combine Id with the other rules: substitution to make two lines match, then MP, MT or DS to use them. When two names appear and an identity links them, ask which substitution would make a premise's antecedent (or a disjunct) look exactly like a line you already have.
Id never cites more than two lines: the identity and the line where a name is replaced.

With identity, the proof system is complete for the whole language of this course: every valid argument with names, predicates, quantifiers and $=$ has a proof. The capstone lesson explains what that claim means.

blocks.html: This course has given you two ways to show an argument is good. One is about truth: truth tables and worlds, with no row or world making the premises true and the conclusion false. The other is about rules: a proof, line by line, from Proofs with Identity and everything before it. Do they always agree? This capstone answers that, drawing also on Counterexample Worlds.

$\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ ("provable") means there is a proof of $\varphi$ from the premises $\Gamma$. $\Gamma \models \varphi$ ("valid") means every row or world that makes $\Gamma$ true makes $\varphi$ true. A system is sound if everything provable is valid, and complete if everything valid is provable. Our rules are both.

Soundness holds because every rule is truth-preserving: each was checked to be a valid form (or an equivalence), and CP, IP and the quantifier rules, with their restrictions, never let a falsehood follow from truths. Completeness is harder and deeper. For statement logic it means the eighteen rules plus CP and IP can reach every tautological consequence. For predicate logic it was proved by Kurt Gödel in his 1929 doctoral thesis: every valid argument of first-order logic has a proof.

head: Says
Direction
blocks.cap: Two properties of a proof system.

items: Soundness: a correct proof guarantees validity, so you never need a truth table to back it up. And if an argument has a counterexample, no proof of it exists, however long you search.
Completeness: if an argument is valid, a proof is out there. If you cannot find one, keep looking, or check validity another way.
Together: $\vdash$ and $\models$ pick out exactly the same arguments.

blocks.title: Use soundness
blocks.q: Someone shows you a "proof" of $p \to q$, $q$, so $p$. What follows?
steps: The argument is invalid (the row $p$ F, $q$ T).
Our system is sound, so no correct proof of it exists.

blocks.title: Use completeness
blocks.q: A truth table shows $(p \lor q) \land \neg p$ implies $q$. Must a proof exist?
steps: The argument is valid.
The system is complete.

blocks.title: Changing the rules
blocks.q: If we added the rule "from $p \to q$ and $q$, infer $p$", what would break?
steps: That rule is affirming the consequent, which is invalid.
It could prove an invalid argument.
blocks.a: Soundness. (Removing a rule, by contrast, can only threaten completeness.)

blocks.html: Swapping the two. Soundness: the rules never prove an invalid argument (provable implies valid). Completeness: the rules can prove every valid one (valid implies provable). A memory aid: soundness protects you from proving falsehoods; completeness promises you are not missing anything.

One limit worth knowing: truth tables decide validity in statement logic mechanically, but for predicate logic there is no general mechanical test that always says "invalid" when it should (Church and Turing, 1936). Completeness guarantees a proof for every valid argument, not a quick way to tell when none exists.
